inline.s: The Buddha, in the Buddha Treasury Sutra
Chapter Seven on Past Times, related the retribution of those who long ago destroyed the Buddha's right Dharma, together with their followers, their supporters, and their donors:
These evil people
who destroy the Buddha's right Dharma

likewise bring grave ruin and calamity to many. Moreover, when these evil people die, they fall into the Avīci hell, lying supine for nine hundred trillion years, lying prone for nine hundred trillion years, lying on the left side
(lying on the left side)
for nine hundred trillion years, lying on the right side
(lying on the right side)

for nine hundred trillion years, burned and scorched on hot iron. Dying and falling from there, they are reborn in the roasting hell, the greatly roasting hell, the living hell, and the black-cord hell, each suffering every torment for the same number of years. Dying in the black-cord hell, they return again to the great Avīci hell.
Śāriputra,
for this reason, whether monastics in the household or those who have left home draw near these people
(the followers of these evil people)
, and the good spiritual friends
(the supporters of these evil people)
, and all the donors of alms
(the benefactors and donors of these evil people)
, in all six hundred and four trillion people who are born and die together with these four teachers
(with these four evil men)
, all undergo burning and boiling in the great hell
. Even so, Śāriputra,

all the households of their good spiritual friends, the households of their donors, their disciples, their teachers, and all who follow along with them, however many there are in that number, are all born in hell

Śāriputra, you are unable to know their number; only the Tathāgata can know it. Together with these evil people they fall into the great Avīci hell, born and dying together, in all six hundred and four trillion people. Thus they turn and suffer for a whole kalpa, and when the great kalpa is about to burn, they remain in hell. Why? Śāriputra, to destroy the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of the Tathāgatas is an exceedingly heavy offense, by no means a light one. When the great kalpa burns, these four evil people and the six hundred and four trillion people pass from this Avīci great hell and are reborn in another region, in the great hell. Why? Śāriputra, their heavy offenses are complete, and the retribution is no small one — in that other region they undergo vast torment for countless hundreds of thousands of millions of koṭis and nayutas of years. When the world arises anew, these four offenders, the six hundred and four trillion people, and all the others whose offenses are not yet exhausted, upon dying there are reborn once more in this great hell here.”
The idiom “to act as the tiger's ghost (
chāng

)” means to serve the tiger as its ghost accomplice. In ancient legend, a person devoured by a tiger would, after death, become such a ghost, deliberately luring other people for the tiger to consume.

blocks.text: A Hidden Current the Buddhist Community Should Take Seriously

inline.s: Master Weixian
December

[Master Weixian] A native of Pengxi, Sichuan, he entered the Sino-Tibetan Buddhist Academy at age fourteen, was greatly esteemed by Master Taixu, and attained deep mastery of Buddhist learning. In his youth his scholarly works made his name known throughout the Buddhist academic world. In the 1950s he was caught up in the political movements and imprisoned for twenty-six years, enduring much suffering behind bars. In prison he never ceased in diligence, delving deeply into the Buddhist canon. Upon his release in the 1980s he became abbot of Ciyun Temple in Chongqing, widely spreading the Buddha-Dharma and its good conditions of karmic affinity. With his profound attainments he preached and transmitted the precepts in temples at home and abroad, earning the deep veneration of the Buddhist community. He served as chairman of the Advisory Committee of the Buddhist Association of China, president of the Chongqing Buddhist Association, and president of the Chongqing Buddhist Academy. He passed away at 4:50 a.m. on February 2, 2013, at Tushan Temple in Nan'an District, Chongqing, at the age of ninety-three.
[Editor's note] This article reveals that China's Benyuan Dharma — whether in doctrine or in funding — derives from the Japanese Benyuan Dharma, and
is a branch center of the Japanese Benyuan Dharma
More and more evidence shows that the impact of this undercurrent is by no means accidental or spontaneous,
but is organized and planned,
backed by
huge sums of money;
and with
the channels and bases
for printing books and recording tapes;
even more so the monks, nuns, and laypeople who preach and stir up enthusiasm
About two years ago (that is, 1997),
the Japanese Benyuan Dharma contacted temples in Jiangxi; if a large ‘Benyuan Dharma’ center could be established, they could remit ten million yuan
These centers, established with funds from the Japanese Benyuan Dharma,
the ‘Benyuan Dharma’ centers,

because the name ‘Benyuan Dharma’ has become so infamous, now change their signs to “Relying on Master Shandao,” “Propagating Master Shandao’s Pure Land thought,” “Propagating Master Shandao’s method of Buddha-recitation,” and “the Shandao lineage,” and do their utmost to conceal their connection with the Japanese Benyuan Dharma. These people harbor crooked and deceitful hearts, acting as though everyone may be fooled and none in the world is as clever as they
(that no one in the world is as clever as they are)
, little knowing that retribution lies behind them, following one after another.
Master Shandao taught: “What is genuine is real, and what is sincere is true. To understand the practice and understanding cultivated through body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings,
it must be done from within a genuine mind.

One may not outwardly display the appearance of goodness, diligence, and progress while inwardly harboring falsity — greed, anger, and wrong views, deceit of every kind, and an evil nature that is hard to moisten, like the viper or the scorpion. Though one engages in the three kinds of action, this is called virtue mixed with poison, and is also called a false practice; it is not genuine karmic action. If one settles the mind and cultivates in this way, even toiling body and mind, day and night through the twelve periods, rushing and doing as though one’s head were on fire, all of it is
(here ‘all’ means the whole of it)
called virtue mixed with poison.
If one seeks to turn back this poison-mixed practice to seek rebirth in that Buddha’s Pure Land, this is utterly impossible.
” (“The Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles”)

[On the remark “a branch center of the Japanese Benyuan Dharma”] In Master Jingkong’s “Buddhist Questions and Answers: Reply to the Seventy-Fourth Session of Hong Kong Practitioners,” there is the following: “Question:
Recently a monk has been lecturing on the Dharma in various parts of China, but in essence he is promoting an evil religion — the Japanese Benyuan Dharma
Their practice is this: if a temple is willing to publicize Japanese Jōdo Shinshū for the Japanese, then they invest ten million renminbi at a stroke
. Second,
if a Chinese layperson is willing to publicize Japanese Jōdo Shinshū for them online, they can provide a monthly salary and bonuses

. The specific working method is that the Chinese layperson comes forward to set up a forum, and people are sent full-time each day to repost the Japanese Jōdo Shinshū posts to the major Pure Land forums.

If this Chinese layperson is very rich in Buddhist knowledge, they can provide a monthly salary of ten thousand yuan (note: the layperson’s monthly salary is ten thousand yuan; if it were a Dharma master, what monthly salary would they provide?)

. The Japanese requirement is to have this seller of Buddhism pretend to be a faithful disciple of Master Yinguang, of Master Jingkong, or of a Vajrayāna guru, to mingle online with ordinary Buddhist friends so that everyone admires their Buddhist learning, and then to lead ordinary Buddhist friends to accept the views of Japanese Jōdo Shinshū. Regarding these matters, please instruct us, Venerable Master.”

[Hongan-ji] Hongan-ji is the head temple of the Jōdo Shinshū Hongan-ji branch of Japanese Buddhism. [Jōdo Shinshū] Also called the Primal Vow sect, it permits monks to marry and have children, and propagates the Benyuan Dharma of “reciting the Name surely brings rebirth, and the evil person is the proper capacity.”
Recently, both from Buddhist periodicals and from actual contact, it has become apparent that
an undercurrent of “learning from Japanese Buddhism and taking the Japanese Buddhist path” has emerged in the Chinese Buddhist world
. This undercurrent strikes on two fronts. First, it undermines the fundamental rule of Chinese Buddhism that monks must observe “monastic dress, vegetarian diet, and celibacy.”

A considerable number of Japanese monastics marry and have children, drink wine and eat meat, wear Western suits, and disregard the precepts — a state of affairs quite welcome to those of our own monks who do not keep the precepts.
The article “The Warning Bell” (published in Taizhou Buddhism,
, issue
, total issue
) exposed: “At present it is found that in the key temples of city
W

four young and middle-aged monastics have already returned to lay life, and the head of the well-known Kai Ru Sutra-Printing Society — the monk Kai Ru of Mount Jiuhua — also returned to lay life last year.” It is said that
in some coastal cities our monks stay in the temple by day and return to their private homes to live as a family by night,
which has an extremely bad social effect.
The second front of attack is
the propagation of Japan’s “Benyuan Dharma”

. It seeks to interfere with and destroy from the spiritual plane, and from the direction and path of studying Buddhism and cultivating. Japanese Buddhism has been transmitted to China for a long time,
and in the 1930s it served the war of aggression against China

. The article “The Warning Bell” disclosed that at the time, in Wuhu, Anhui, “there was a Japanese Buddhist temple on Zhong’er Street, with Japanese-style lanterns hanging at the gate bearing the red characters ‘Higashi Hongan-ji,’ and inside lived a Japanese monk and his whole family. The Japanese monk often carried a leather drum and beat it as he walked along the street. It is said this was so in every other city the Japanese occupied; they served along with the army, specially performing rites of deliverance for the dead Japanese.

At that time, when Japan invaded China, they called it a ‘holy war’; killing for the ‘holy war’ was no crime, and after death the soul would rise to the Buddha’s realm. Those who killed many Chinese and thereby earned merit could have their famed name entered in a ‘shrine.’ After the War of Resistance ended, the unpopular Japanese Buddhism vanished from the mainland of China.
Who would have thought this specter would be reanimated from the dead by ‘a certain group
(namely Master Huijing, Master Jingzong, and others)
’ — is this not absurd?
The layman Zheng Songying of Shanghai pointed out in the article “Eradicating the Three Evils by Refuting the False and Upholding the True,” published in Taizhou Buddhism: “Japa
n’s ‘Benyuan Dharma’ has recently reached China — a sect that looks like the Pure Land school, yet runs wholly counter to the Buddha’s Dharma, misleads sentient beings, and does great harm; it is
, once seen through,
in fact an evil demon within the teaching

! It proclaims that as long as one hears the name of Amitabha Buddha and can arouse faith, one has obtained the ‘identity card’ to the Land of Bliss and will be reborn there for certain! There is no need to continue Buddha-recitation or practice, and no matter how one dies, and even without deathbed assistance, one will certainly be reborn!” “‘Benyuan Dharma’ requires only a single ‘faith,’ with no need at all for ‘practice’ — relying wholly on the power of another and not on self-power — is this still Buddhism?” In fact, in the late Qing and early Republican period, the layman Yang Renshan, through the Japanese Buddhist scholar Nanjō Bun’yū, introduced a great many Buddhist scriptures, and already criticized and rejected the ‘Benyuan Dharma.’ (See the “Classified Compilation on Expounding the Teaching” in the Continuation of the Great Treasury
the twelfth item of Layman Yang’s compilation). Not a single one of the great masters of the Pure Land school in modern and contemporary China has advocated the ‘Benyuan Dharma.’
More and more signs prove that
the impact of this undercurrent is by no means accidental or spontaneous,
but is organized and planned,
supported by
huge sums of money;
and with
the channels and bases
for printing books and recording tapes;
even more so the monks, nuns, and laypeople who preach and agitate
. About two years ago,
the Japanese Benyuan Dharma contacted temples in Jiangxi; if a large ‘Benyuan Dharma’ center could be established, they could remit ten million yuan

. At that time they too had doubts about the claim that the ‘Benyuan Dharma’ required only a single ‘faith’ and could dispense with Buddha-recitation and practice. But they also wanted to use this huge sum to build a center and afterward still spread the orthodox Pure Land school. They wrote to ask the elder layman Zheng Songying of Shanghai. In his reply Elder Zheng pointed out: “To act thus would be to take the ground wrongly — one should firmly decline and not accept it.” Only then did they let it drop.
It has now been verified that there are very many bases propagating the ‘Benyuan Dharma,’ and several of them carry on the activity frequently.
The article “The Warning Bell” says: “In the past two years, the
Japanese Jōdo Shinshū Benyuan Dharma in Taiwan
has repeatedly mailed books and promotional materials to Buddhist organizations in Anhui, and some Buddhists have already been influenced by it.”
There are two young and middle-aged monastics who claim to be from Mount Jiuhua, propagating Japanese Buddhism in various cities. One of them, glib of tongue, is called ‘Master Sheng Su (
now renamed Master Jingzong
),’ and he exploits people’s reverence for Mount Jiuhua as a Buddhist holy ground and their respect for its monks, finding connections to help them arrange venues for preaching,
so that lay devotees of little experience and monastics who do not keep the precepts are delighted

During the Spring Festival this year, Master Sheng Su and the other monk accompanied a Taiwanese nun down the mountain to preach again. From Xuancheng to Wuhu they spent a day preaching and a day discussing,
and afterward were questioned by the Municipal CPPCC and the Bureau of Religious Affairs

, in the first half of the year, this undercurrent also penetrated the southwest, and Chongqing in particular felt its influence most. Not only did it mail large quantities of books such as the “Amitabha Calling Series” from Cangtangyan,

of Xuanzhou in Anhui, and from the “Gift of the Bodhi Center of the Ciyuan Group” in Dezhou, Shandong, by Jue Xing and others; that summer it also sent a young monk into the Chongqing city area, very secretively, without revealing the name of his home temple or his Dharma name. He stayed at a layman’s home and organized one group after another of followers to hear him extol the ‘Benyuan Dharma,’ and the bewitched grew in number day by day, until the lay practitioners of the Pure Land method in Chongqing split into two factions. Some laypeople who upheld the Pure Land method of the “two powers” (the Buddha’s power and self-power) raised many questions to this monk; his answers were unclear, and he even flew into a rage and said: “You will fall into hell! Into hell! Into hell!”
Judging from the situation described above, if this undercurrent is allowed to grow and spread unchecked, it will gravely corrode, and perhaps even destroy, the whole of Buddhism.

(Original editor’s note: The Benyuan Dharma distorts the three Pure Land sutras and the one treatise, advocating that there is no need to recite scriptures, observe the precepts, arouse the bodhi mind, or cultivate the six perfections and the myriad practices of the bodhisattva. This wholly violates Buddhist doctrine and the Mahāyāna spirit of transcending the world while yet entering the world; it is
in fact
an external path attached to the Buddha,
which should arouse the height attention and resistance of the Buddhist community, and we also hope the relevant government departments will take note
